summary.text:
A clean, orthodox district treasury report. Four PWLB maturity loans totalling £35.46m at rates 3.21%, 3.40%, 3.53% and 3.48% — the whole HRA Self-Financing settlement of 28 March 2012 — and our engine ties every row exactly on count, principal, rate and maturity date. Beyond that the council has no non-HRA external borrowing and did not draw in the quarter.

On the DMO's premature repayment curve today, all four loans price below par; the indicative net discount is £6.3m, about 17.8% of principal. The earliest event in the book is the 2030 maturity — £8.87m at 3.21% — three years and seven months from today. On the current 5-year certainty rate (5.34%) refinancing that at par would run about £189k a year more in interest.

Non-HRA CFR grew from £1.167m to a forecast £16.99m in the year — a nearly fifteen-fold rise — funded entirely internally, and the council's stated position is that it will continue to borrow internally until rates reduce further. Investments at 30/9/25 were £61.655m, outperforming SONIA by 22 basis points and on track for a £2.18m outturn against a £2.02m budget.

The paper is the Q2 mid-year 2025/26; the 2025/26 annual outturn was published in July 2026 and is on our queue but not yet ingested. The loan-book reconciliation and today's break-cost picture are stable and do not depend on which paper is read; the CFR and investment-yield lines will have moved.

Contacts are named without email addresses — Antony Baden as S151 (front sheet) and Sian Southerton as report contact (page 7, phone only). Draft is written but blocked on an address.

officer.body:
Hi [NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are a few thoughts based on your Q2 2025/26 mid-year report, the one that went to Full Council on 7 January. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your 2025/26 annual outturn went to Audit on 13 July and we haven't ingested it yet, so we've stuck to the parts of the picture that don't move between reports.

A cross-check first. Your Appendix 2 §1.4 lists four PWLB maturity loans totalling £35.46m at 3.21% (28 March 2030), 3.40% (2035), 3.53% (2050) and 3.48% (2062). Our engine holds the same four loans at a weighted 3.4049% — an exact match on count, principal, rate and maturity date for every row. That's the HRA Self-Financing settlement of 28 March 2012 and it hasn't moved since.

The reason we wrote is where those four rates sit against the curve today.

On the DMO's premature repayment curve at yesterday's PM fixing, all four of your loans price below par. The indicative net position is a discount of about £6.3m, roughly 17.8% of principal. The two long-dated loans do most of the work — the 2062 at 3.48% shows about £2.8m below par and the 2050 at 3.53% about £2.3m — and even the 2030 at 3.21% shows about £317k. These are indicative and only the DMO can quote a settlement; we don't model MRP or accounting treatment either, so whether any of this is worth acting on turns on replacement cost and reserve headroom that we can't see from here.

The other angle is timing. The 2030 loan — £8.870m at 3.21% — matures on 28 March 2030, about three years and seven months from today. On today's 5-year certainty rate of 5.34%, refinancing that £8.87m at par would run about £189k a year more in interest than the current coupon. On the MUFG glide-path in your paper (5-year at 4.30% by mid-2026 falling to 4.10% by 2028) it would run about £80k-100k more; the 5-year has held above that forecast so far. Either way the direction at that maturity is up, not down. It's the first event in your book and worth having marked in the calendar even if there's nothing to decide today.

Your daily-priced position is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. The sector context for what the PWLB is actually lending each month sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July's lending was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, so thin activity and thin months are usually when inter-authority money gets dear.

On training, four courses fit Arun. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator speaks directly to the discount arithmetic above. PWLB repayment structures is the primer on how maturity, annuity and EIP loans move at rescheduling. Reading the Metrics dashboard covers the sector-wide indicators. And Money Market Funds (CNAV / LVNAV / VNAV) for the £16.8m MMF slice of your investment portfolio. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
